explore.title: Explore Mars
explore.intro: Mars from orbit. Major features are labelled at their official (IAU) positions. Jezero Crater, in orange, is where Copernico works: explore its surface and plan walks there.
explore.coverageNote: HiRISE-derived 1 m elevation model. Outside this outline Copernico does not compute routes.
explore.guidedDescription: Landing site → Three Forks sample depot → Hawksbill Gap delta front, returning to the start.
explore.why: A 45 km crater that held a lake about 3.5 billion years ago; the river delta it left is still preserved on its western side. NASA's Perseverance rover has explored it since February 2021, collecting rock samples for possible return to Earth.

route.title: Plan a Marswalk
route.intro: Five steps: choose the stops, calculate, review, simulate, then save or share. Routes stay inside the coverage outline.
route.empty: No waypoints yet. Choose a start point.
route.picking: Click the terrain to add a point (Esc to stop)
route.gridUnavailable: The Jezero terrain grid is not available. Route planning is disabled.
route.unresolvedList: Rocks smaller than ~1.5 m, relief below ~0.5 m, DTM artifacts, loose or dust-covered voids, soil strength, and suit limits at Mars gravity.
route.assumptionsNote: Slope limit, speeds and EVA limits come from lunar (Apollo/Artemis) sources and are assumptions for Mars. S = sourced, A = assumption.
route.profileCursor: Elevation profile: position along the route
route.profileHint: Elevation profile (m). Hover or use the arrow keys to follow the route on the map.
route.playHint: Cinematic walk of the selected route, with the EVA clock and the slope underfoot; touch the map to stop.
route.playReduced: Disabled because reduced motion is on.

steps.reviewHint: Calculate a route to see distance, time, the daylight timeline, the elevation profile and science stops nearby.
steps.simulateHint: Once a route is ready: a cinematic walk with an EVA clock and the slope underfoot.
steps.saveHint: Once a route is ready: save it in this browser, copy a share link, export GeoJSON or CSV, or print a briefing.

metrics.walkbackRule: Smallest margin along the route: EVA limit − (time elapsed + time to walk back to the start + suit ingress). Lunar-derived rule, labelled as an assumption for Mars.

explain.DETOUR_AVOIDS_STEEP_TERRAIN: The lower-risk route is {{extra}} longer than the shortest feasible route and avoids {{steep}} of 15–20° slopes and {{moderate}} of 10–15° slopes. Its steepest terrain is {{lrMax}}, versus {{shMax}} on the shortest route (slope from the HiRISE-derived 1 m elevation model, 10 m baseline).
explain.SAME_AS_SHORTEST: The lower-risk and shortest feasible routes are essentially the same here.
explain.ROUGH_TERRAIN: {{distance}} crosses rough micro-relief (1 m slopes above 25° in part of the cell).
explain.LOW_THERMAL_INERTIA: {{distance}} crosses low thermal inertia (< 100), which can indicate loose material. Source resolution is 100 m.
explain.WALKBACK_EXCEEDED: Walk-back rule violated after {{at}}: elapsed time + return along the path + 30 min ingress exceeds the 8 h EVA limit.
explain.EVA_NOMINAL_EXCEEDED: Estimated duration {{duration}} exceeds the 6 h nominal EVA.
explain.WALK_RADIUS_EXCEEDED: The route goes {{distance}} from the start, beyond the {{limit}} walking radius used for lunar walking EVAs.
explain.OUTSIDE_COVERAGE: Waypoint {{n}} is outside the route-planning coverage.
explain.WAYPOINT_NOT_TRAVERSABLE: Waypoint {{n}} is on terrain that exceeds the constraints ({{reason}}).
explain.DISCONNECTED: Leg {{leg}} cannot be completed: a {{barrier}} barrier separates the points. The nearest reachable point is {{gap}} from the target.

environment.title: Conditions and time
environment.intro: What is calculated, what was measured, and when. There is no live weather for Jezero.
environment.noDaylight: The Sun does not reach {{min}}° on this sol.
environment.measurementsPending: MEDA measurements are published on the PDS about 3–4 months after they are taken. The newest released data end on 2026-05-13 (sol 1859). They are being prepared for this app.
environment.noLive: No mission publishes live weather for Jezero. Any value shown here is dated.
environment.lighting: Scene lighting uses this calculated Sun direction. No atmospheric scattering or terrain shadows are modeled.
environment.airTemp: Air temperature near the mast (min … max)
environment.medaWhere: Measured at the rover position on that sol: elevation {{elevation}} m, {{distance}} from the Jezero landing site. Pressure changes with elevation.
environment.medaCaveat: Median of MEDA air temperature sensors 1–3 on the mast; local values that may include rover thermal influence. Not live weather.
environment.medaRange: Across {{n}} sols with data: nightly lows {{lowMin}} to {{lowMax}} °C, daily highs {{highMin}} to {{highMax}} °C, mean pressure {{pMin}}–{{pMax}} Pa.
environment.nowLine: Right now at Jezero (calculated): sol {{sol}}, {{time}} LTST.

timeline.title: EVA timeline
timeline.daylightOk: Back {{margin}} before the Sun drops below {{deg}}° (at {{time}} LTST).

timeline.daylightBadStart: The Sun is below {{deg}}° at departure ({{time}} LTST). Start later in the morning.

welcome.title: Plan a walk on Mars
welcome.lede: Copernico combines data from five NASA missions to help future astronauts plan a safe walk on Mars, and do science along the way.

mars.title: Mars
mars.body: The whole planet, its major features, and the way into Jezero Crater.

surface.title: Surface
surface.body: Perseverance in 3D, science sites and maps of what the ground is made of.

marswalk.title: Marswalk
marswalk.body: Plan a walk in five steps, check daylight and the walk-back margin, then simulate it.

conditions.title: Conditions
conditions.body: Time, Sun, season and the weather Perseverance measured.

panoramas.title: 360° views
panoramas.body: Real panoramas taken by Perseverance, and a tour that flies between them.

welcome.later: The ? button at the top has the tour, a demo mode and “Things to try”, a checklist of everything Copernico can do. Unsure about a word?

planet.title: This is Mars
planet.body:
A 3D model of Mars built from NASA orbiter images and elevation data. Drag to turn it; scroll or pinch to zoom. Major features are labelled at their official positions, and Jezero Crater, in orange, is where everything in Copernico happens.
The stars and the Milky Way behind it are where they really are, seen from Mars at the planned walk time.
Press Next, or let the tour do a step for you with “Do it for me”. Esc leaves the tour at any time.

panels.title: Five tabs, one per activity
panels.body: Mars (the planet), Surface (Jezero up close: the rover, maps of the ground, science sites), 360° views (real panoramas and a tour between them), Marswalk (plan and simulate a walk) and Conditions (time, Sun and weather data). Each tab takes the camera to its place. Click the open tab again to hide the panel.

jezero.title: Fly to Jezero Crater
jezero.body: Jezero is a 45 km crater that held a lake about 3.5 billion years ago. NASA's Perseverance rover has explored it since 2021. This button flies you there and opens the Surface tab.

area.title: Jezero up close
area.body:
The outlined rectangle is the only place with 1-metre terrain detail (from the HiRISE camera); walks are planned inside it.
The orange line is the real path Perseverance drove. Purple dots are science sites: click one to read about it.

guided.title: Step 1: choose the stops
guided.body: Pick points on the map, type coordinates, or load the guided walk: landing site → sample depot → delta front, and back. You can set how long the crew works at each stop.

calculate.title: Step 2: calculate
calculate.body: The planner checks every 5 m square of terrain, avoids slopes steeper than 20° and finds the path with the lowest estimated risk. It takes about half a second.

results.title: Step 3: review the plan
results.body:
Distance, estimated walking time, how much the path climbs, and the steepest slope on it.
“Walk-back margin” is the time left before the 8-hour suit limit, always keeping enough time to walk back. Green means the plan fits.

alternatives.title: Safer or shorter?
alternatives.body: Copernico computes two routes: the lower-risk one, which avoids steeper ground, and the shortest one. Switch between them here; “Why this route” below explains the difference in plain words.

timeline.title: When to walk
timeline.body: The walk on a clock: walking in green and time at each stop in amber. The yellow curve is the Sun's height in the sky; the line below says whether the crew is back before the Sun gets low.

profile.title: Ups and downs
profile.body: Height along the route. Colours show slope: green gentle, yellow moderate, orange steep. Move the mouse over it, or use the arrow keys, and a white dot follows on the map.

science.title: Science on the way
science.body: Science sites close to your route, with the extra walking time each one would add. “Add stop” puts it in your plan and recalculates.

layers.title: Map tools
layers.body: Always on the map: Layers (each with an ⓘ about its data source and limits), the compass to face north, and 2D/3D to look straight down or at an angle.

play.title: Step 4: simulate the walk
play.body: A cinematic walk along the route, with an EVA clock, the slope underfoot and an arrival at each stop. The same button appears on the map whenever a route is ready. Touch the map to stop it.

missions.title: Step 5: save and share
missions.body: Save the plan in this browser, copy a link that opens the same plan for anyone, or export it as GeoJSON, a spreadsheet (CSV) or a printable briefing.

help.title: Help is always here
help.body:
From ? you can resume this tour, replay one chapter, run it hands-free as a demo, or open “Things to try”, a checklist of everything Copernico can do.
Remember: routes show lower estimated risk from orbital data, never guaranteed safety.

panoramas.title: Real 360° views
panoramas.body: Ten panoramas stitched from Perseverance's Mastcam-Z images, placed where they were taken. Open one, or let “Tour all” travel through them in mission order, flying the rover's real drive between them.

panoramaView.title: Look around
panoramaView.body: Drag to look around and scroll to zoom. The bar shows the sol, the Mars season and what lies in each direction; the mini-map shows where you are looking. The hatched button shows which part was filled in (the rover's own deck, below the camera). Esc closes it.

rover.title: Perseverance
rover.body: The rover in 3D at its latest published position. Below the button, chips put its full drive, the sample sites and the Ingenuity helicopter flights on the map.

ground.title: What the ground is made of
ground.body: Maps from orbit: mineral signals from the CRISM spectrometer, thermal inertia (sand versus rock), slope and height. A legend on the map explains the colours.

inspect.title: Inspect any point
inspect.body: Click the ground anywhere in Jezero: the card shows its height, slope and ground type, and whether a crew could walk there. You can add the point to a walk from the card.

pois.title: Science sites
pois.body: Places where Perseverance worked, with why they matter and what a crew could investigate. “Show on map” flies there; “Add as stop” puts the site in your walk.

conditions.title: When to walk
conditions.body: The planned EVA start drives the Sun in the scene, the stars and the walk timeline: change it here and watch the light move. Below are the Sun height, the season, the daylight window and the latest weather measured by Perseverance (not live).

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.intro: Every technical word in Copernico, in plain language.

marswalk.def: A walk outside the habitat or vehicle in a spacesuit. EVA means extravehicular activity.

jezero.def: A 45 km wide crater on Mars (18.4°N, 77.5°E) that held a lake about 3.5 billion years ago. A river delta of layered sediments remains on its western side.

perseverance.def: NASA's Mars 2020 rover. It landed in Jezero on 18 February 2021 and collects rock samples. The orange line on the map is the path it drove.

sol.def: A day on Mars: 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds. Sol numbers here count from Perseverance's landing day (sol 0).

ltst.def: Time of day at Jezero set by the real Sun: 12:00 LTST is when the Sun is highest. A Mars hour is 1/24 of a sol, about 61.6 Earth minutes.

ls.def: Where Mars is on its orbit around the Sun, used as its season: 0° starts northern spring, 90° summer, 180° autumn and 270° winter.

plannedEva.def: The start time of the walk you are planning. It sets the Sun's position, the scene lighting and the stars shown. Change it in Conditions.

evaLimit.def: The planning maximum for one walk (8 hours, from NASA lunar walk plans) and the time to get back inside (30 minutes). Both are assumptions for Mars.

walkback.def: At every point of the walk, the time left before the EVA limit after counting the time needed to walk back and get inside. If it is negative, the plan does not fit.

slope.def: How steep the ground is, in degrees, measured over 10 m. Bands: up to 10° gentle, 10–15° moderate, 15–20° steep.

slopeLimit.def: Ground steeper than 20° is treated as not walkable. The value comes from lunar walking experience and is an assumption for Mars.

lowerRisk.def: The lower-risk route accepts a little more distance to avoid steeper or rougher ground; the shortest route only respects the hard limits. Neither guarantees safety: small rocks and soft soil cannot be seen from orbit.

coverage.def: The rectangle where a 1-metre elevation model from HiRISE exists. Routes are computed only inside it.

elevation.def: Height above Mars's “sea level”, the areoid: a reference surface from MOLA and gravity data. Jezero's floor is about 2,500 m below it.

thermalInertia.def: How quickly the ground heats up and cools down, measured from orbit by THEMIS. Low values suggest loose sand or dust; high values suggest rock.

crism.def: A spectrometer on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Its maps show signals of minerals such as carbonates, clays and olivine. They are indicators: confirming a mineral needs its full spectrum.

hirise.def: The sharpest camera orbiting Mars, on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Copernico uses its 25 cm images and the 1 m terrain model made from them.

ctx.def: The Context Camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, about 5 m per pixel. It gives the wider view of the crater.

mola.def: The laser altimeter on Mars Global Surveyor. It measured the shape of the whole planet; Copernico uses it for global relief.

viking.def: A global colour map of Mars made from the Viking orbiters (1976–1980). The colours are enhanced, not exactly what the eye would see.

meda.def: Perseverance's weather station. Copernico shows the latest released measurements with their date; no mission publishes live weather from Jezero.

reach.def: The area a crew can walk to from the start and still walk back within the time limit, in one-hour bands.

detour.def: The extra distance and walking time needed to visit a science site, compared with the same leg without it.

dwell.def: Minutes the crew spends working at each stop (20 by default). You can change it for each stop in Plan.

daylight.def: Whether the Sun stays more than 10° above the horizon for the whole walk, so the crew works and returns in good light.

panorama.failed: The panorama could not be displayed on this device.
panorama.canvasLabel: 360° panorama. Drag or use the arrow keys to look around; + and − zoom.
panorama.caption: A real photo mosaic by Perseverance's Mastcam-Z, sol {{sols}} ({{date}}), in natural colour.
panorama.measured: Compass and horizon measured by matching the skyline to the terrain model (median error {{residual}}°). The sky above the photo is a plain gradient; black areas have no data.

hud.noSamples: No samples were collected within 600 m of this stop.
hud.unimagedNote: About {{percent}}% of the image was not photographed: the rover’s own body blocks the camera’s view down. Those areas are filled smoothly from the surrounding photo (no invented detail) and are always marked: slightly darker, with faint diagonal lines.
hud.minimap: Map: your position, the direction you are looking and nearby panoramas

about.van-zyl: Perseverance parked at this overlook for 13 days in April 2021 (sols 53–64) while the Ingenuity helicopter made its first flights over the field in front of it.
about.crocodile-bridge: A stop on the crater rim, west of the delta, where Perseverance waited out the 2025–2026 solar conjunction, when the Sun sits between Earth and Mars and the team pauses commanding.

tour.label: Auto-tour
tour.startHint: Travel through every 360° view in mission order, flying straight from one to the next
tour.startAll: Tour all {{count}} 360° views along the path
tour.skip: Go on to the next stop

intro.butler-landing: You are standing where Perseverance landed on 18 February 2021, on the flat floor of Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed on Mars. This was one of its first full looks around: dark, wind-worn rocks and sand, with the cliffs of an old river delta about 2.5 km to the west and the crater rim on the horizon.
intro.van-zyl: You are on a low rise of the crater floor, about 100 m from the landing spot. The flat, rock-strewn ground in front of you was chosen as the "airfield" of the Ingenuity helicopter.
intro.seitah-1: You are on Artuby Ridge, a low ridge of the crater floor about 1 km south-west of the landing site, looking into Séítah ("amid the sand" in Navajo): a field of sand ripples and rock ridges that Perseverance explored in 2021.
intro.wildcat-ridge: You are at the foot of the river delta, at a gap in its front called Hawksbill Gap, about 2.7 km north-west of the landing site. The layered cliffs around you are the edge of the fan of sediment that an ancient river built into the lake.
intro.enchanted-lake: You are at the base of the delta front, about 2.8 km west of the landing site, where the sediment carried by the ancient river met the floor of the lake. The rocks here were laid down in water, layer by layer.
intro.three-forks: You are on the flat ground at the foot of the delta, about 2.5 km west of the landing site. The low ridge on the horizon is the front of the delta: the edge of the fan of sediment that an ancient river built into the lake.
intro.belva: You are on top of the delta, about 5 km north-west of the landing site, at the edge of Belva, an impact crater about 900 m wide that formed later and cut into the delta.
intro.bright-angel: You are in Neretva Vallis, the ancient river channel that fed the lake, at the north-western edge of the delta, about 9 km from the landing site. Among the pale rocks around you is the one the team named "Cheyava Falls".
intro.witch-hazel-hill: You are high on the inner slope of the crater rim, at Witch Hazel Hill, about 10 km west of the landing site. These rocks are older than the lake: some were broken or melted by the impact that made Jezero.
intro.crocodile-bridge: You are on the rim of Jezero Crater, about 12 km west of the landing site, after the climb Perseverance made through 2024 and 2025. The rocks up here formed long before the lake, and were reshaped by the impact that made the crater.

kind.tube: The core inside its sample tube
kind.closeup: The rock beside the core, close up

samplePhoto.title: Sample {{n}} · {{name}}
samplePhoto.listNote: Each sample with NASA’s photo of where it was drilled (or of the core in its tube). Click a photo to enlarge it.

game.title: Jezero Sample Run
game.tagline: Drive Perseverance over the real terrain of Jezero Crater and collect the samples it took, at the places where it took them.
game.failed: The game could not start: the terrain or the rover model is missing, or this device cannot display WebGL 2.

floor.name: Crater floor
floor.desc: Five sites near the landing site: the volcanic rocks of Jezero's floor.

delta.name: Delta front
delta.desc: Five sites at the foot of the ancient river delta, then leave the tubes at the Three Forks depot.

margin.name: Delta top
margin.desc: Five sites over about 2.5 km on top of the ancient delta, west to the margin unit.

how.drive: Drive with W A S D or the arrow keys. Hold Shift to go faster (it uses more battery).
how.core: Stop inside a ring and press Space (or E): the arm comes down and cores the sample.
how.slope: Slopes over 30° stop the rover, as they would stop the real one.
how.power: The battery recharges slowly from the rover's nuclear power source (its MMRTG), faster when stopped.
how.keys: C camera · M map · F laser · P photo · Esc pause · drag to look around · scroll to zoom.
how.laser: Stopped near rocks, centre one in the view and press F: SuperCam’s laser tells what it is made of and earns science points.
how.photo: Press P for photo mode: pick a rover camera, frame the shot and keep it in your gallery.

hazards.sand: Soft sand (dark, rippled ground): the wheels slip and dig in. Do not stop or boost in it. If you get stuck, back out slowly. Spirit was trapped for good in 2009.
hazards.rocks: Sharp rocks: driving over boulders fast wears the wheels, as it punctured Curiosity’s. Below 50 % the rover is slower.
hazards.tilt: Slopes: over 30° the rover stops, uphill or sideways.
hazards.storm: Dust storms: the haze closes in for half a minute. Follow the compass and the map.

game.realNote: The terrain is the real one, from the HiRISE 1 m elevation model, out to the crater rim on the horizon. The ground textures are cut from Perseverance’s own Mastcam-Z panoramas, and the sample sites are real (NASA/JPL MMGIS). Rocks, small craters, dust and tracks are generated. To fit in minutes, the game drives about 140 times faster than Perseverance (top speed 4.2 cm/s).

prompt.stopToCore: Stop to core the sample at {{name}}
prompt.holdToDrop: Press Space to leave the tubes at the Three Forks depot
prompt.toDepot: All samples in: take them to the Three Forks depot
prompt.steep: Too steep: Perseverance is designed for slopes up to 30°
prompt.edge: Edge of the 1 m terrain model: turn back
prompt.power: Battery flat: recharging from the MMRTG…
prompt.stuck: Stuck in soft sand! Back out slowly (S), as Opportunity escaped Purgatory dune in 2005
prompt.tiltBlocked: Side slope over 30°: the rover would tip over. Turn and go another way
prompt.stormSoon: A dust storm is coming: visibility will drop
prompt.storm: Dust storm: AutoNav drives slower while it cannot see far
prompt.rocks: Sharp rocks: slow down to save the wheels ({{pct}}% left)
prompt.sand: Soft sand: the wheels slip {{pct}}%. Do not stop or boost here
prompt.laserReady: F: analyse this rock with the SuperCam laser
prompt.laserDone: This rock has already been analysed: aim at another one

why.atmospheric: The rock crumbled during coring, so this tube holds a sample of the Martian air instead.
why.igneous: Igneous rock, crystallised from molten rock. Dated in a laboratory on Earth, it would tell when Jezero's floor formed.
why.sedimentary: Sedimentary rock, laid down in water by the river and lake that once filled Jezero. Rocks like this are the most likely to keep signs of ancient life.
why.mixed: Grains of sedimentary and igneous rock, carried by the river from across the region.
why.regolith: Regolith: loose rock and dust from the surface. It shows how Martian soil would affect astronauts and their equipment.
why.carbonate: Silica-cemented carbonate: minerals that grow in water and can trap traces of the environment they formed in.

complete.title: Mission complete
complete.real: Perseverance took these samples between sol {{first}} and sol {{last}}: {{sols}} sols, about {{months}} months on Earth.

collection.locked: Core it in the {{mission}} mission to add it to your collection.
collection.rocksIntro: Stop near a rock, centre it in the view and press F: the laser reads what it is made of.

gallery.empty: No photos yet. Press P while driving (or Photo mode here) to take one: they are kept in this browser.

options.hazardsHelp: Soft sand where the rover can get stuck, and sharp rocks that wear the wheels when driven over fast.
options.stormsHelp: Storms that hide the terrain for half a minute; the rover drives slower in them.
options.resetHelp: Clears your collection, science points and best times (photos stay).

basalt.name: Basalt-like lava rock
basalt.desc: Pyroxene and plagioclase: rock that cooled from lava, like the Máaz formation that covers Jezero’s floor.

olivine.name: Olivine-rich rock
olivine.desc: Green olivine crystals that settled in a thick body of magma, like the Séítah formation. Water later altered them.

sulfate.name: Sulfate salts
sulfate.desc: Calcium and magnesium sulfates left by water that soaked through the rock and evaporated.
sulfate.hint: Light-toned rocks, especially at the delta front.

clay.name: Clay-bearing mudstone
clay.desc: Fine sediment laid down in the ancient lake. Clays form in water and can preserve organic molecules.

carbonate.name: Carbonate
carbonate.desc: Magnesium and iron carbonates, minerals that grow in water. On Earth such rocks can trap signs of life.
carbonate.hint: Delta, and especially the margin unit.

silica.name: Silica (opal)
silica.desc: Almost pure silicon dioxide, deposited by water. It is very good at preserving microscopic fossils.
silica.hint: Rare: light rocks of the delta top.

meteorite.name: Iron–nickel meteorite
meteorite.desc: A piece of an asteroid’s metal core that fell on Mars. Curiosity and Perseverance have both found some.

photo.title: Photo mode

about.natural: The colours as they would look to the eye on Mars.
about.whiteBalance: As if lit by daylight on Earth: NASA releases images like this so geologists can read rock colours.
about.enhanced: A contrast and colour stretch, as in NASA’s enhanced-colour images.
about.navcam: The black-and-white navigation cameras on the mast.
about.hazcam: The fisheye hazard cameras on the body, near the wheels.

photo.hint: Drag to turn the view · scroll to zoom in close.
